explanations.explanation: Naaman, commander of Aram's army, has everything going for him, and then the verse says he was “…but he was a leper.” That little "but" is carrying the WHOLE building. Rank, respect and victories on one side, leprosy on the other. I bet he'd have handed back a medal or two for clear skin.

Verse 1 says nothing about Naaman's eyes. Blindness isn't the problem the text gives him. It says he was a leper. One word like that sits on the back end of a long list of good things and changes the whole picture.

The text never says Naaman can't walk. He's called a mighty man of valor, and I'd say that sounds like a man who gets around. The thing working against him is leprosy. It shows up right at the end of the verse, after all the good news.

The girl says, “If only my master would go to the prophet who is in Samaria, he would cure him of his leprosy.” She's the one taken from Israel, and she's the one who points to help. Small voice, big news. Nobody in that house had thought to ask her, and I bet it wasn't a short list of people who'd tried.

It's true, actually. The girl tells her mistress, “If only my master would go to the prophet who is in Samaria, he would cure him of his leprosy.” She speaks up for the man whose household she serves. So the text has her pointing Naaman toward the prophet, not away from him.

The king of Aram says he'll send Naaman with a letter to the king of Israel. That's the land the young girl was taken from, and it's where she said the prophet was. So the whole trip points back at her words. Send a man with a letter to the right address, and sometimes that's half the miracle.

Verse 5 gives a different address: the letter goes to the king of Israel. Judah isn't in the story. A letter sent to the wrong king would be like me stamping a cookie and hitting the wrong tray. The text keeps the destination plain: Israel.

Egypt isn't anywhere in this story. The king of Aram says he will send Naaman with a letter to the king of Israel (2 Kings 5:5). That fits what the girl said about a prophet in Samaria. Naaman's trip stays in the land she came from.

The letter says, “With this letter I am sending my servant Naaman, so that you may cure him of his leprosy.” Short, direct, no small talk. It's a letter that gets right to the point. The king of Israel reads it and doesn't take it well.

The letter does ask exactly that. It says, “With this letter I am sending my servant Naaman, so that you may cure him of his leprosy.” That's the whole request, in plain words. It's the reason the king of Israel tears his clothes next.

The king of Israel says, “Surely you can see that he is seeking a quarrel with me!” A quarrel is a fight. He reads a letter asking for a cure and hears a challenge. Friend, I've read a text message wrong before, but never a whole kingdom's worth.

A treaty is peace on paper, and that's not what the king of Israel hears. He says, “Surely you can see that he is seeking a quarrel with me!” That's the opposite of a treaty. He thinks he's being picked on.

Trade isn't what's on the king's mind. After reading the letter he says the man is seeking a quarrel with him. A quarrel is a fight, and he sounds sure of it. I think he's more upset about what he can't do than what he's being offered.

explanations.answer: That there is a prophet in Israel
explanations.explanation: Elisha, the man of God, tells the king, “Please let the man come to me, and he will know that there is a prophet in Israel.” The king of Israel tore his clothes, and Elisha just says send him over. I think Elisha is pretty calm about it. No panic, just an invitation.

explanations.answer: That the king of Israel is wise
explanations.explanation: Elisha never says anything about the king's wisdom. He says, “Please let the man come to me, and he will know that there is a prophet in Israel.” The king's the one tearing his clothes. Elisha is the one who steps in.

Army never comes up in Elisha's message. He says, “…he will know that there is a prophet in Israel.” Naaman is the army man here, and he's about to need something no army can give him. Elisha's point is the prophet.

That's not what happens. Naaman stands at the door, and Elisha sends a messenger instead. The messenger says, “Go and wash yourself seven times in the Jordan, and your flesh will be restored, and you will be clean.” Elisha never comes out in this scene.

Elisha stays inside and sends a messenger. The messenger says, “Go and wash yourself seven times in the Jordan, and your flesh will be restored, and you will be clean.” So the instructions come second-hand. I think a man with a full set of horses and chariots might have expected a handshake.

explanations.answer: Call on the LORD and wave a hand over the spot
explanations.explanation: Naaman says, “I thought that he would surely come out, stand and call on the name of the LORD his God, and wave his hand over the spot to cure my leprosy.” He had a whole scene pictured in his head. Then a messenger gave him a river instead. Friend, I've pictured plenty of things that came out different, and mine usually just involve burnt edges.

explanations.answer: Walk with him to the Jordan and wash him there
explanations.explanation: Naaman never says that. He expected Elisha to “…come out, stand and call on the name of the LORD his God, and wave his hand over the spot to cure my leprosy.” He wanted something to happen right where he stood. The Jordan was Elisha's instruction, not his picture.

explanations.answer: Send word to the king to bless him first
explanations.explanation: Naaman doesn't mention a blessing from the king. What he pictured was Elisha coming out, calling on the name of the LORD his God and waving a hand over the spot. The king isn't in that picture at all. The only thing he asked for was the prophet himself.

explanations.answer: He'd do a great thing so why not this simple one
explanations.explanation: His servants say, “My father, if the prophet had told you to do some great thing, would you not have done it?” Then they add, “How much more, then, when he tells you, ‘Wash and be cleansed’?” They're calling him "My father" while telling him he's overthinking it. That's some brave, kind talking.

explanations.answer: The rivers of Damascus are just too far away
explanations.explanation: Distance isn't their argument. Naaman complained about the Abanah and Pharpar, the rivers of Damascus, and his servants answer a different way. They say, “…if the prophet had told you to do some great thing, would you not have done it?” Their point is that it was easy, not that anything was far.

explanations.answer: The prophet might come out if he waits longer
explanations.explanation: They don't tell him to wait for anything. They say that if the prophet had asked him to do some great thing, he would have done it. Then they say, “How much more, then, when he tells you, ‘Wash and be cleansed’?” They want him to act, not stand around at the door.

explanations.answer: Like the flesh of a little child
explanations.explanation: The text says his flesh “…was restored and became like that of a little child, and he was clean.” Nothing left behind, nothing half done. That's what happens when he does what the man of God said. Seven dips, one big change.

explanations.answer: Clean except for one small spot
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't leave any spot. After the seventh dip, his flesh “…was restored and became like that of a little child, and he was clean.” No patch left over. Whole job done.
Scars aren't mentioned. The text says his flesh “…was restored and became like that of a little child, and he was clean.” That's a lot more than scars healing over. Restored means restored.

explanations.answer: There is no God in all the earth except in Israel
explanations.explanation: Naaman says, “Now I know for sure that there is no God in all the earth except in Israel.” This is the same man who left angry at the door of Elisha's house. Now he's back, standing in front of Elisha. Seven dips later, he doesn't just say thanks. He says WHO he now knows is God.

explanations.answer: The waters of Israel are better than any in Aram
explanations.explanation: Naaman did argue about rivers earlier, but that's not what he declares here. He says, “Now I know for sure that there is no God in all the earth except in Israel.” He's talking about God, not water. The river was the road, and God was the destination.

explanations.answer: Elisha is greater than any king in the world
explanations.explanation: Naaman doesn't say anything about Elisha being greater than a king. His declaration is, “Now I know for sure that there is no God in all the earth except in Israel.” The focus lands on God, not the prophet. Elisha is the one who points the way.

That's not what happens. Elisha says, “As surely as the LORD lives, before whom I stand, I will not accept it.” Naaman urges him, and Elisha still refuses. A man could walk out of there with a fortune and chose not to.

Elisha turns it down. He says, “As surely as the LORD lives, before whom I stand, I will not accept it.” Naaman keeps urging, and Elisha keeps refusing. I can't tell you how rare it is to turn down a gift that big, friend.

explanations.answer: As much soil as two mules can carry
explanations.explanation: Naaman says, “…please let me, your servant, be given as much soil as a pair of mules can carry.” He wants soil to take home. Then he says he'll never again make a burnt offering or a sacrifice to any other god but the LORD. Two mules' worth of dirt. I think that's a man who plans to take something of Israel home with him.

explanations.answer: Twelve stones from the middle of the Jordan
explanations.explanation: Naaman doesn't ask for stones. He says, “…please let me, your servant, be given as much soil as a pair of mules can carry.” His request is about soil, and mules do the hauling. No river rocks in this story.

explanations.answer: Cedar logs from the forests of Lebanon
explanations.explanation: Cedar logs never come up. Naaman asks, “…please let me, your servant, be given as much soil as a pair of mules can carry.” It's dirt, not lumber. Two mules would have a lot to carry already.

Naaman says, “For your servant will never again make a burnt offering or a sacrifice to any other god but the LORD.” That's a big change from the man who showed up at the door. He's making a promise about who he'll worship. It comes right after he asks for the soil.

Naaman doesn't name Baal at all. He says he'll never again make a burnt offering or a sacrifice to any other god “…but the LORD.” His promise is about the LORD. The only other god he mentions by name is Rimmon, in the next verse.

Dagon doesn't come up in this story. Naaman says, “…your servant will never again make a burnt offering or a sacrifice to any other god but the LORD.” He names the LORD as the only one. He leaves the other names out.

Elisha says, “Go in peace.” That's his whole answer after Naaman asks the LORD to forgive him in this matter. Short and simple, and it comes before Naaman travels off. The text doesn't add anything more to it.
He does say that. Elisha answers, “Go in peace.” Those are his words right after Naaman asks the LORD to forgive him in this matter. Then Naaman heads off.

explanations.answer: Run after Naaman and get something from him
explanations.explanation: Gehazi, Elisha's servant, says, “As surely as the LORD lives, I will run after him and get something from him.” He uses his master's words and then announces his own plan. I think that should have been the red flag. Elisha said no to the gift, and Gehazi decided to go get it anyway.

explanations.answer: Go tell Elisha to take the gift after all
explanations.explanation: Gehazi never plans to talk to Elisha. He says, “I will run after him and get something from him.” The plan is to go after Naaman himself. Elisha isn't part of it.

explanations.answer: Follow Naaman to make sure he gets home
explanations.explanation: Gehazi's plan has nothing to do with getting Naaman home safely. He says, “I will run after him and get something from him.” He's not running to help. He's running to collect.

explanations.answer: Give silver and clothing for two young men from the sons of the prophets
explanations.explanation: Gehazi says, “My master has sent me to say, ‘Look, two young men from the sons of the prophets have just now come to me from the hill country of Ephraim. Please give them a talent of silver and two sets of clothing.’” Elisha never sent him. That's the story he invents on the road. Friend, that's a lot of detail for a made-up errand.

explanations.answer: Come back to the house so Elisha can bless you and your servants again
explanations.explanation: Gehazi doesn't say anything about a blessing. His claim is that two young men from the sons of the prophets came to Elisha, and that Elisha wants a talent of silver and two sets of clothing for them. It's a request for supplies. And Elisha didn't send him with any message.

explanations.answer: Elisha has changed his mind and will take the gold you brought after all
explanations.explanation: Gehazi never says Elisha changed his mind. He asks for a talent of silver and two sets of clothing for two young men from the sons of the prophets. Naaman had offered much more, but Gehazi asks for less. His story is built around a smaller request.
Gehazi asks for a talent of silver. Naaman says, “Please, take two talents.” And he urged Gehazi to accept them. So Gehazi walks away with double what he asked for.

Naaman gives MORE. Gehazi asked for a talent of silver, and Naaman insisted, “Please, take two talents.” He even tied the silver up in two bags with two sets of clothing. I'd say that's a pretty generous man.

Gehazi says, “Your servant did not go anywhere.” That's his answer to Elisha's question, “Gehazi, where have you been?” After running down a chariot, taking silver and storing it in the house, that's what he came up with. I think Elisha didn't need the explanation.

explanations.answer: He was down at the Jordan
explanations.explanation: Gehazi doesn't mention the Jordan. When Elisha asks, “Gehazi, where have you been?” he replies, “Your servant did not go anywhere.” He gives a flat denial. No place named at all.

explanations.answer: He was with the sons of the prophets
explanations.explanation: Gehazi had used the sons of the prophets in his story to Naaman, but he doesn't use them here. When Elisha asks where he's been, Gehazi says, “Your servant did not go anywhere.” That's the whole answer. He denies the trip entirely.

Elisha says, “Therefore, the leprosy of Naaman will cling to you and your descendants forever!” The same leprosy that Naaman left behind in the Jordan lands on Gehazi. It's a heavy moment. I think this one hurts, so I'll let it stand as it is.

Miriam, Moses' sister, did have leprosy once (Numbers 12:10). But that's not the name Elisha says here. He says, “…the leprosy of Naaman will cling to you and your descendants forever!” This one is about Naaman's leprosy.

Uzziah, a king of Judah, had leprosy until the day he died (2 Chronicles 26:21). But Elisha doesn't name him. He says, “…the leprosy of Naaman will cling to you and your descendants forever!” The name in this story is Naaman.
